title: Dual-Faraday-laser-pumped cesium beam clock with $7.7\times 10^{-13}/\sqrtτ$ frequency stability
authors: Xiaomin Qin, Suyang Wei, Haijun Chen, Yufei Yan, Qiang Wei, Hangbo Shi, Zhiyang Wang, Zheng Xiao, Zijie Liu, Tiantian Shi, Jingbiao Chen
abstract: Compact cesium beam clocks are major frequency references for deployable timing systems. However, further improvement of their short-term frequency stability is limited by the clock signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Although two-laser optical pumping can increase the effective atomic utilization, the achievable clock SNR has long been limited by laser-induced frequency-to-amplitude noise conversion. Here, we demonstrate a compact dual-Faraday-laser-pumped (DFP) Cs beam clock enabled by a low-frequency-noise atom-referenced laser architecture. The intracavity Faraday anomalous dispersion optical filter provides inherent alignment to the Cs D$_2$ resonances, while modulation transfer spectroscopy offers suppressed frequency noise and drift. The resulting laser system supports robust turnkey operation with a Lorentzian linewidth of 2.12 kHz. The DFP Cs clock achieves a clock SNR of 46,365 in a 1-Hz bandwidth and a fractional Allan deviation of $7.7\times 10^{-13}/\sqrtτ$ , with Hadamard deviation reaching $7.7\times 10^{-15}$ at 10,000 s. This work pushes the fractional frequency stability of a compact Cs beam clock into the $10^{-13}/\sqrtτ$ regime, providing a pathway toward high-performance Cs frequency references for field-deployable precision timing, navigation, and synchronization.
summary: The authors present a compact Dual-Faraday-laser-pumped (DFP) Cesium beam clock designed to achieve superior frequency stability for portable timing systems. By integrating advanced laser stabilization techniques like Modulation Transfer Spectroscopy with Faraday filtering, they successfully suppressed noise sources inherent in previous designs. This results in record short-term stability of $7.7	imes 10^{-13}/\sqrt{	au}$, advancing the state-of-the-art for field-deployable atomic clocks.
main_problem: The primary goal is improving the short-term frequency stability of compact Cesium (Cs) beam clocks for use in field-deployable timing systems, overcoming limitations imposed by laser noise.
main_result: The developed Dual-Faraday-laser-pumped (DFP) Cs clock achieved a fractional Allan deviation of $7.7	imes 10^{-13}/\sqrt{	au}$, pushing stability into the highly desirable $10^{-13}/\sqrt{	au}$ regime.
method: The technique involves using two lasers stabilized via Modulation Transfer Spectroscopy (MTS) and employing an intracavity Faraday anomalous dispersion optical filter (FADOF) for inherent resonance alignment.
model_or_system: The system is a compact Cs beam clock utilizing two distinct laser pumping transitions ($	ext{F}=4 	o 	ext{F}'=5$ and $	ext{F}=3 	o 	ext{F}'=2$). It relies on low-frequency-noise, atom-referenced lasers stabilized through complex optical feedback loops.
key_observables: Clock SNR (46,365 in 1 Hz), fractional Allan deviation ($7.7	imes 10^{-13}/\sqrt{	au}$), and Hadamard deviation ($7.7	imes 10^{-15}$ at 10,000 s).
important_parameters: Lorentzian linewidth of 2.12 kHz; stability improvement from $1.1 	imes 10^{-12}/\sqrt{	au}$ (SFP) to $7.7 	imes 10^{-13}/\sqrt{	au}$ (DFP).
main_assumptions: The primary limitation addressed is the conversion of laser frequency noise into fluorescence noise in standard two-laser pumping schemes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy level diagrams for single vs. dual Faraday pumping, the experimental schematic of the DFP clock setup, and plots detailing stability measurements (ADEV/HDEV) versus averaging time ($	au$).
paper_structure: The paper details the physical system components, describes the advanced stabilization techniques (MTS, FADOF), presents quantitative performance metrics comparing different pumping schemes, and concludes with future optimization paths.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant engineering achievement in precision measurement using atomic physics principles. The successful suppression of laser noise to reach $10^{-13}/\sqrt{	au}$ stability is highly relevant for quantum sensing and metrology applications that require robust field operation.
